title: How Much You Should Save for Healthcare Costs in Retirement
description: Budgeting for the $315,000 expense that Medicare doesn't fully cover.
content:
Many Americans believe that once they hit 65, healthcare becomes free thanks to Medicare. This is a dangerous myth. Medicare has premiums, deductibles, co-pays, and massive coverage gaps (like dental, vision, and hearing). According to Fidelity's annual retiree healthcare cost estimate, a 65-year-old couple retiring in 2024 needs approximately **$315,000** (after tax) to cover medical expenses in retirement. This does not even include Long-Term Care. This guide helps you budget for the single largest line item in your retirement plan.

Key Takeaways

  • Medicare isn't Free: Part B (Doctors) premiums are ~$175/month per person. Part D (Drugs) and Medigap (Supplemental) add hundreds more. You will likely spend $500-$800/month per couple just on premiums.
  • The 'Donut Hole': Prescription drug costs can spiral. While recent laws capped out-of-pocket drug costs at $2,000/year starting in 2025, that is still a $2,000 annual liability you must fund.
  • Excluded Care: Medicare does not cover Dental, Vision, or Hearing Aids. You must self-insure these or buy expensive private plans.
  • Long-Term Care (LTC): The $315k estimate excludes nursing homes. Assisted living costs ~$5,000/month. You need a separate strategy (LTC Insurance or Home Equity) for this.

Why It Matters (US Context)

High-income retirees face 'IRMAA' (Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount). If your retirement income is high (>$200k couple), the government charges you extra for Medicare premiums. Roth accounts help avoid this surcharge by keeping taxable income low.

The Cost Breakdown (Per Person)

Where does the money go?

1. Premiums (The Monthly Bill)

  • Part B: ~$175/mo (deducted from Social Security).
  • Part D (Rx): ~$50/mo.
  • Medigap (Plan G): ~$150/mo.
  • Total Fixed Cost: ~$375/month per person ($9,000/year per couple).

2. Out-of-Pocket (The Usage)

Even with Medigap, you have small deductibles. Plus Dental/Vision costs. Budget $2,000/year per person for 'Usage'.

3. Inflation

Medical inflation runs higher than CPI (often 5-6%). Your healthcare budget at age 85 will be double what it is at age 65.

How to Fund It

  1. The HSA Strategy: The Health Savings Account is the ultimate tool. Max it out every year while working. Invest it. By 65, a $100k HSA can pay your Medicare premiums tax-free.
  2. Roth Conversions: To avoid IRMAA surcharges, convert Traditional IRA money to Roth in your 60s. This lowers your 'Reported Income' in your 70s, keeping your Medicare premiums at the base rate.
  3. The 'Medical Sinking Fund': If you don't have an HSA, earmark a specific portion of your 401(k) (e.g., $300k) as 'Medical Only'. Do not count this money toward your lifestyle spending/travel budget.
  4. Delay Social Security: The higher check from delaying to 70 helps offset the rising cost of Part B premiums.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the 'Gap'?

If you retire at 55 but Medicare starts at 65, you have a 10-year gap. You must pay full price for ACA insurance ($1,500/mo). You need a massive bridge fund for this.

Does Medicare cover nursing homes?

No. It covers 'Skilled Nursing' for rehab (up to 100 days). It does not cover 'Custodial Care' (living there). That is out of pocket or Medicaid (if you are broke).

Is Medigap necessary?

Highly recommended. Original Medicare has a 20% coinsurance with no cap. If you have a $100k surgery, you owe $20k. Medigap creates a cap. Do not go without it.
